hints: Think about where the heartbeat has to start to make blood flow in the correct direction - which upper chamber receives deoxygenated blood first and needs to contract first?
walkthrough:
Pacemaker Position Makes Functional Sense**
The sinoatrial node (SAN) is the pacemaker. It generates the wave of excitation, so it must sit in the muscle of an atrium where that wave can immediately spread across both atria to cause them to contract together.

Pinpoint the Chamber**
That chamber is the right atrium, near where the vena cava enters. Saying just atrium is not precise enough - you need wall / muscle of the right atrium for the mark.
Final answer: In the wall / muscle of the right atrium.

hints: The SAN is in the atrium wall, so its excitation spreads across atrial muscle first - what stage of the cardiac cycle describes contraction of those upper chambers?
walkthrough:
Follow the Excitation Wave**
When the SAN fires, the wave of excitation spreads out across the muscle of both the left and right atria. Muscle responds to excitation by contracting.

Name the Stage Correctly**
Contraction is called systole. So contraction of the atrial walls pushed blood into the ventricles is atrial systole. Do not confuse this with ventricular systole, which comes later.
Final answer: Atrial systole / contraction of the atria.

hints: If excitation spread straight from atria to ventricles, they would all contract together - what structural barrier stops this and forces a detour?
Think about the only allowed route through that barrier and how a short pause there gives the atria time to finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
walkthrough:
Why a Delay Is Essential**
Atria must finish contracting and push all blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract. If ventricles contracted at the same time, ventricular volume and pressure would be too low for effective ejection.

The Insulating Layer Forces a Detour**
A ring of non-conducting fibrous tissue sits between the atria and ventricles. It cannot conduct excitation, so the wave from the SAN cannot pass directly into ventricular muscle.

AVN Delay Then Rapid Spread**
The impulse is therefore picked up by the atrioventricular node (AVN), which imposes a delay of about 0.1 s. It then passes rapidly down the bundle of His and Purkyne tissue to the base of the ventricles, triggering ventricular systole from the bottom up after atrial systole is complete.

Final answer: AVN delays the impulse from the SAN / atrial muscle; non-conducting fibrous tissue prevents direct spread to ventricles so impulse must pass via AVN then to Purkyne tissue for ventricular contraction.

hints: After Purkyne tissue fires, ventricular muscle contracts and ventricular pressure rises sharply - which valves guard the exits to the large arteries and must open to let blood out?
walkthrough:
Link Impulse to Ventricular Contraction**
Impulse from AVN to Purkyne tissue causes the ventricle walls to contract - ventricular systole. Pressure in the ventricles rises above pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery.

Which Valves Open for Ejection?**
That high pressure forces open the valves at the base of the two large arteries to allow ejection. These are the semilunar valves - the aortic valve on the left and the pulmonary valve on the right. The atrioventricular valves are closed at this point to prevent backflow to the atria.
Final answer: Semilunar valves (aortic valve and pulmonary valve).
